body:
Bioremediation: reducing pollution through living systems

Bioremediation uses organisms or their biological activities to remove, transform, immobilise or reduce the harmful effects of environmental contaminants. Microorganisms are particularly important because some bacteria and fungi can use certain pollutants as sources of carbon or energy.

Oil-derived hydrocarbons and other suitable organic pollutants may undergo microbial degradation. Depending on the pollutant and environmental conditions, degradation may produce simpler and less harmful substances. However, complete removal is not guaranteed. Some pollutants are resistant to biodegradation, and partial breakdown can sometimes produce intermediate substances that also require attention.

Organic pollutants and heavy metals behave differently

A crucial distinction concerns the chemical nature of the contaminant. Organic pollutants may be broken down because microorganisms can alter their molecules through metabolism.

Heavy metals, such as lead and cadmium, are chemical elements. They cannot be destroyed by biological degradation. Biological processes may instead change their chemical form, immobilise them or help concentrate them for removal. Thus, stating that microorganisms completely decompose heavy metals is incorrect.

Major approaches

  • Microbial bioremediation: uses bacteria, fungi or other microorganisms to act on contaminants.
  • Phytoremediation: uses plants and associated biological processes to remove, stabilise or transform certain pollutants.
  • Biostimulation: encourages useful microorganisms already present at a site by improving suitable environmental conditions.
  • Bioaugmentation: introduces suitable microorganisms to assist a treatment process.

Bioremediation may be undertaken at a contaminated location, called in situ treatment, or after contaminated material has been moved to a treatment facility, called ex situ treatment. These terms describe where treatment occurs, not the identity of the organism.

Microorganisms in sewage treatment

Sewage contains water, suspended solids, organic matter and microorganisms, some of which may cause disease. Treatment reduces the pollution load before water is discharged or reused. Biological treatment is particularly important for reducing biodegradable organic matter.

Primary treatment

Primary treatment mainly uses physical processes, including screening and settling, to remove floating debris and suspended or settleable solids. The settled material forms primary sludge. The remaining liquid proceeds to further treatment.

Secondary treatment

Secondary treatment uses microorganisms to consume biodegradable organic matter. In a common activated-sludge process, air is supplied to support aerobic microorganisms. These microorganisms form aggregates called flocs, which contain bacteria and may be associated with fungal filaments.

As the microorganisms consume organic matter, the wastewater's biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) generally decreases. BOD indicates the amount of dissolved oxygen required by microorganisms to break down biodegradable organic matter under specified test conditions. A higher BOD usually indicates a greater biodegradable organic pollution load.

After biological treatment, the microbial flocs settle to form activated sludge. Some of this sludge may be returned to the aeration stage, while additional sludge can be treated in anaerobic digesters. Anaerobic digestion may produce methane-rich biogas.

Biological treatment does not automatically remove every pathogen, toxic chemical, dissolved salt or other contaminant. Further treatment, including disinfection or additional purification, may be needed depending on the intended use or discharge requirements.

Primary treatment is mainly physical removal of solids. Secondary treatment is mainly biological reduction of organic matter. Anaerobic sludge digestion treats suitable sludge and can produce biogas.

Prelims focus

  • Bioremediation uses living systems to treat contaminants.
  • Phytoremediation uses plants; microbial bioremediation uses microorganisms.
  • Biostimulation supports existing microorganisms; bioaugmentation introduces suitable microorganisms.
  • Primary sewage treatment is mainly physical; secondary treatment is mainly biological.
  • Higher BOD generally indicates a greater biodegradable organic pollution load.
  • Trap: Heavy metals cannot be destroyed by microbial decomposition.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 10, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', §§10.3–10.4; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 12, 'Biotechnology and Its Applications', introductory applications; National Human Genome Research Institute, 'Synthetic Biology', section on environmental applications, consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Microorganisms play an important role in wastewater treatment.

title: Bioremediation and Biological Wastewater Treatment

body:
Why agricultural biotechnology is needed

Plant breeding aims to develop crop varieties with useful characteristics such as improved yield, resistance to particular pests or diseases, nutritional quality and tolerance to environmental stress. Conventional breeding uses genetic variation, crosses between suitable parents and selection of offspring with desirable characteristics.

Modern agricultural biotechnology adds methods that help produce planting material or identify desirable plants more effectively. Two important examples are plant tissue culture and marker-assisted selection. Neither method necessarily requires introducing foreign DNA into a plant.

Plant tissue culture

Plant tissue culture involves growing plant cells, tissues or small plant parts under controlled conditions on an appropriate nutrient medium. The starting plant material is called an explant.

The principle underlying plant regeneration is totipotency: under suitable conditions, certain living plant cells have the genetic information and developmental capacity needed to regenerate a complete plant. Regeneration nevertheless depends on the cell type, plant species and culture conditions.

From a small plant part to many plants

A small piece of suitable plant material can be used to obtain plantlets through tissue culture. These plantlets must subsequently become established under ordinary growing conditions. This transition is called acclimatisation or hardening.

Producing many plantlets from a relatively small amount of starting material is called micropropagation. It is particularly useful where rapid multiplication of desirable planting material is needed, including crops and horticultural plants such as banana and ornamental plants such as orchids.

Meristem culture and disease-free planting material

Meristem culture uses actively growing plant tissue, often from a shoot tip. It can help obtain plants free from certain viral infections because some meristematic regions may contain little or no detectable virus. However, disease-free status is not guaranteed merely because a plantlet has been produced in tissue culture. Appropriate testing and healthy starting material remain important.

Tissue-cultured plants produced by clonal multiplication are generally intended to resemble the selected parent. Nevertheless, genetic variation can sometimes arise during culture; this is known as somaclonal variation. Therefore, tissue culture does not guarantee that every plantlet is genetically identical under all circumstances.

Marker-assisted selection

Marker-assisted selection (MAS) uses identifiable DNA differences called molecular markers to help select plants carrying a desirable gene or genomic region. A useful marker is associated with the trait of interest and has been shown to predict it reliably in the breeding material concerned.

For example, a breeder may cross 2 rice plants, one possessing a useful resistance characteristic and another possessing desirable yield or grain-quality characteristics. Molecular markers can help identify offspring carrying the desired resistance-associated genetic region. The breeder can then select promising plants for further evaluation.

The essential distinction is that MAS detects and selects existing genetic variation. It does not itself insert, remove or edit DNA. The desired trait must still be confirmed because a marker is an indicator, not automatically proof of satisfactory performance under all field conditions.

Comparison of the 2 methods

FeatureTissue cultureMarker-assisted selection
Primary purposeGrow or multiply plant materialSelect plants with desirable genetic regions
Underlying principlePlant growth and regenerative capacityAssociation between DNA markers and traits
Common applicationRapid multiplication of selected plantsImproved precision in breeding decisions
Foreign DNA required?NoNo

Prelims focus

  • Totipotency is a central principle of plant regeneration through tissue culture.
  • An explant is the starting plant material used in tissue culture.
  • Micropropagation enables rapid multiplication of selected plants.
  • Meristem culture can help produce virus-free planting material, subject to verification.
  • MAS uses DNA markers associated with desirable traits.
  • Trap: MAS identifies genetic characteristics; it does not edit a plant's DNA.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 9, 'Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production', §§9.2 and 9.4; Indian Council of Agricultural Research, 'Crop Cultivars Developed through Molecular Breeding', 2nd edition, Introduction, consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Plant tissue culture can multiply desirable planting material.

title: Plant Tissue Culture and Marker-Assisted Breeding

body:
Biofertilisers improve nutrient availability

A biofertiliser contains beneficial living microorganisms that help improve nutrient availability to plants through their biological activities. Biofertilisers do not work in exactly the same way as chemical fertilisers, which directly supply specified nutrients in chemical forms.

Some biofertiliser organisms fix atmospheric nitrogen, while others help plants obtain nutrients such as phosphorus from the soil. Their effectiveness depends on the crop, soil environment, microbial survival and other conditions.

Important organisms and their functions

Rhizobium and root nodules

Species of Rhizobium form beneficial associations with the roots of many leguminous plants. They inhabit specialised structures called root nodules and convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms that enter plant nitrogen metabolism. The plant provides carbohydrates and a suitable habitat to the bacteria.

This relationship is an example of symbiosis, in which both partners benefit. Nitrogen fixation should not be confused with photosynthesis: atmospheric nitrogen is converted into biologically usable nitrogen compounds, not into sugars.

Free-living and associated nitrogen-fixing bacteria

Azotobacter and Azospirillum are important examples of bacteria associated with biological nitrogen fixation. Unlike the familiar Rhizobium association with legume root nodules, these organisms do not require that same type of legume nodule relationship.

Cyanobacteria

Some cyanobacteria can fix atmospheric nitrogen. Anabaena and Nostoc are important examples. Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria can contribute to soil fertility, particularly in waterlogged agricultural environments such as rice fields.

Mycorrhiza

A mycorrhiza is a beneficial association between a fungus and plant roots. The fungus helps the plant absorb nutrients, especially phosphorus, and can improve access to water under suitable conditions. The plant supplies photosynthetically produced carbohydrates to the fungal partner. Members of the fungal genus Glomus are familiar textbook examples.

Biofertiliser, organic manure and chemical fertiliser

These terms should not be used interchangeably. Biofertilisers rely on beneficial microorganisms. Organic manure consists largely of decomposed plant or animal material that adds organic matter and nutrients. Chemical fertilisers supply nutrients in manufactured chemical forms. A farmer may use these inputs in different combinations according to crop and soil requirements.

Biopesticides and biological control

A biopesticide uses a biological source or biological substance to control a pest. Biological pest control also includes the use of predators, parasites and other natural enemies.

Bacillus thuringiensis, commonly called Bt, is a bacterium that produces insecticidal proteins active against particular susceptible insects. Bt-based microbial products can be used against suitable insect pests. The proteins are not equally effective against every insect species.

The fungus Trichoderma is used in biological management of certain plant diseases. Some Trichoderma species can suppress harmful fungi through competition and other biological interactions.

Useful natural predators also contribute to biological control. Ladybird beetles can feed on aphids, while dragonflies feed on insects including mosquitoes.

Biological agentPrincipal roleExample
RhizobiumSymbiotic nitrogen fixationLegume root nodules
GlomusMycorrhizal nutrient uptakePhosphorus absorption
Bacillus thuringiensisMicrobial insect controlSusceptible caterpillar pests
TrichodermaBiological disease managementCertain fungal plant diseases

Bt biopesticide versus Bt crop

A Bt-based biopesticide uses a microbial product for pest control. A Bt crop, such as Bt cotton, is a genetically modified plant that carries selected Bt genes and produces specific insecticidal proteins within the plant. Both involve Bt biology, but they are not the same agricultural technology.

Biological control can reduce reliance on some synthetic pesticides, but it may not eliminate the need for other pest-management measures. Pest specificity, weather, microbial survival and resistance development can affect performance.

Prelims focus

  • Rhizobium is associated with nitrogen-fixing nodules of leguminous plants.
  • Azotobacter and Azospirillum are associated with biological nitrogen fixation.
  • Anabaena and Nostoc are examples of cyanobacteria.
  • Mycorrhizal fungi, including Glomus, help plants obtain phosphorus.
  • Bt is Bacillus thuringiensis; Trichoderma is a fungus used in biological disease management.
  • Trap: A Bt microbial pesticide and a genetically modified Bt crop are different products.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 10, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', §§10.5–10.6; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 12, 'Biotechnology and Its Applications', §12.1; NCERT, Science, Class 8, ch. 2, 'Microorganisms: Friend and Foe'.]

pictures.caption: Different beneficial microorganisms support different nutrient pathways.

title: Biofertilisers, Biopesticides and Biological Pest Control
